'''Dorothy Toplitzky Blum''' (February 21, 1924 – October 1, 1980)<ref name=hnf>{{cite web|url=http://blog.hnf.de/die-lady-von-der-nsa/|title=Die Lady von der NSA|language=German|publisher=Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum|date=January 22, 2016|accessdate=April 13, 2016}}</ref> was an American [[computer scientist]] and [[cryptanalyst]]. She worked for the [[National Security Agency]] and its predecessors from 1944 until her death in 1980.

== Early life ==
Dorothy Toplitzky was born in 1924 in New York City to Austro-Hungarian immigrant parents.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Die Lady von der NSA HNF Blog|url=https://blog.hnf.de/die-lady-von-der-nsa/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-08-30|website=blog.hnf.de|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160401150851/http://blog.hnf.de/die-lady-von-der-nsa/ |archive-date=2016-04-01 }}</ref>

== Career ==
After graduating from [[Brooklyn College]] in 1944, she joined the cryptologic unit of the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Dorothy T. Blum|url=https://www.nsa.gov/About-Us/Current-Leadership/Article-View/Article/1622398/dorothy-t-blum/|access-date=2021-08-30|website=www.nsa.gov|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-09-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210918134547/https://www.nsa.gov/About-Us/Current-Leadership/Article-View/Article/1622398/dorothy-t-blum/|url-status=dead}}</ref> This unit focused on [[cryptanalysis]], the study of analyzing information systems to gain access to hidden aspects of systems,<ref>{{Citation|title=Cryptanalysis|date=2021-08-04|url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cryptanalysis&oldid=1037148731|work=Wikipedia|language=en|access-date=2021-08-30}}</ref> in this case, the Axis powers' encrypted messages. After [[World War II]], she worked for the United States Armed Forces Security Agency and later the National Security Agency (NSA).<ref name=":0" />

During her time at the NSA in the 1950s, Blum was tasked with "keep[ing] abreast of the latest advances in the field of computing" and recommended computer technologies that could be adapted for [[cryptanalysis]] and communications intelligence.<ref name=":0" /> This included her use of the FORTRAN programing language<ref>{{Citation|title=Fortran|date=2021-08-22|url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fortran&oldid=1040059288|work=Wikipedia|language=en|access-date=2021-08-30}}</ref> beginning three years before its public release in 1957.<ref name=":0" /> She wrote computer software for the NSA and spearheaded the effort to teach NSA employees to write cryptanalytic programs.<ref name=":0" />

Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Blum continued to work in the field of computer science, helping to design the NSA's computer systems and automate processes. In 1972, she became the chief of the NSA Computer Operations Organization (C7), the only woman at the time in the organization's management hierarchy.<ref name=":0" /> She was appointed chief of Plans and Project Development Organization (T4) in the Telecommunications and Computer Services Organization in 1977.<ref name=":0" /> She was also involved in the Women in NSA (WIN) group.<ref name="nsa">{{cite web|date=January 15, 2009|title=Dorothy T. Blum (1924–1980)|url=https://www.nsa.gov/about/cryptologic_heritage/hall_of_honor/2004/blum.shtml|publisher=National Security Agency|accessdate=April 13, 2016}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
Blum died from cancer on October 1, 1980, aged 56.<ref name="50th">{{cite press release|url=https://www.nsa.gov/public_info/_files/crypto_almanac_50th/Dorothy_Toplitzky_Blum.pdf|publisher=[[National Security Agency]]|date=March 5, 2010|title=Cryptologic Almanac 50th Anniversary Series – Dorothy Toplitzky Blum: A Pioneer Computer Scientist|accessdate=April 13, 2016|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151026025616/https://www.nsa.gov/public_info/_files/crypto_almanac_50th/Dorothy_Toplitzky_Blum.pdf|archivedate=October 26, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1980/10/04/dorothy-t-blum-56-nsa-systems-analyst/cc04bc1f-d29c-4d88-9762-f18d3ff533dc/|publisher=[[The Washington Post]]|date=October 4, 1980|title=Dorothy T. Blum, 56, NSA Systems Analyst|accessdate=April 7, 2026}}</ref> An internal award at the NSA - the Dorothy T Blum Award for excellence in employee personal and professional development - was named after her.<ref name=":0" /> In 2004, she was inducted into the [[NSA Hall of Honor]].<ref name=nsa /> An official NSA biography states that, in her 36-year career, Blum "significantly changed the way NSA did cryptanalysis."<ref name=":0" /> She was also elected one of the top 100 "most outstanding women in the federal government."<ref name="women">{{cite web|date=January 15, 2009|title=Dorothy Blum|url=https://www.nsa.gov/about/cryptologic_heritage/women/honorees/blum.shtml|publisher=National Security Agency|accessdate=April 13, 2016}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
In 1950, she married NSA mathematician Joseph Blum,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Joseph Blum Papers|url=https://www.american.edu/library/archives/finding_aids/blum_fa.cfm|access-date=2021-08-30|website=American University|language=en}}</ref> and they later had a son, David Blum.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Obituaries|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2002/04/13/obituaries/448aa69e-9631-40d1-8997-db07b81f942a/|newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref>
